## Abstract

BACKGROUND: Algeria has no documented national companion-animal cancer registry, and limited information is available on tumors encountered in veterinary practice or reaching histopathological confirmation. This dual-source descriptive study combined two independently analyzed components: a histopathology-based descriptive case series of diagnostic tumor submissions from dogs and cats, and a cross-sectional questionnaire survey of veterinarians practicing in Algeria. The first component characterized tumors reaching histopathological confirmation, whereas the second examined practitioner-reported tumor patterns, perceived diagnostic-resource availability, and self-reported preparedness.

RESULTS: The histopathology-based case series comprised 86 tumor submissions from 81 animals accrued between March 2022 and March 2025. Mammary tumors were the largest category (43/86; 50.0%), followed by cutaneous/subcutaneous tumors (20/86; 23.3%); 80 tumors (93.0%) were classified as malignant. Among 162 questionnaire responses collected between October 2024 and May 2025, 111 respondents selected "dogs and cats" as their main animal group. Mammary tumors were reported by 109 respondents (98.2%), cutaneous/subcutaneous tumors by 79 (71.2%), and canine transmissible venereal tumor (CTVT) by 54 (48.6%); multiple categories could be reported. The most frequent self-reported preparedness rating was "Moderately prepared" (52/111; 46.8%), while 99 of 110 respondents with valid data (90.0%) rated diagnostic resources as either "Insufficient" or "Not at all satisfactory." Mammary and cutaneous/subcutaneous tumors ranked first and second in both sources, whereas the rankings of the remaining categories differed. Because the sources represented different populations, analytical units, denominators, and diagnostic pathways, the comparison was restricted to an exploratory descriptive assessment and was not interpreted as evidence of differences in population-level tumor occurrence.

CONCLUSIONS: This study provides an initial structured account of companion-animal tumor documentation in Algeria.

Background: Our work aims to assess the health status of a stray cat population through an epidemiological and clinical study of urban stray cats in the Batna province (north-eastern Algeria) by determining the prevalence of various diseases and risk factors.
Methods: Overall, 270 stray cats were captured and examined. Faecal samples were collected and examined using various coprological techniques. For retroviruses, serological tests were performed on blood samples using FeLV and FIV rapid diagnostic kits. The prevalence of various conditions (gastrointestinal parasitic infections, retroviruses, systemic diseases, eye disorders, etc.) was studied according to the age, sex and health status of the cats examined.

## Abstract

### Background

Algeria has no documented national companion-animal cancer registry, and limited information is available on tumors encountered in veterinary practice or reaching histopathological confirmation. This dual-source descriptive study combined two independently analyzed components: a histopathology-based descriptive case series of diagnostic tumor submissions from dogs and cats, and a cross-sectional questionnaire survey of veterinarians practicing in Algeria. The first component characterized tumors reaching histopathological confirmation, whereas the second examined practitioner-reported tumor patterns, perceived diagnostic-resource availability, and self-reported preparedness.

### Results

The histopathology-based case series comprised 86 tumor submissions from 81 animals accrued between March 2022 and March 2025. Mammary tumors were the largest category (43/86; 50.0%), followed by cutaneous/subcutaneous tumors (20/86; 23.3%); 80 tumors (93.0%) were classified as malignant.

This study provides an initial structured account of companion-animal tumor documentation in Algeria. The partial agreement between the two sources, together with unfavorable diagnostic-availability ratings, suggests potential gaps between clinical recognition, histopathological confirmation, and systematic recording. Standardized submission and coding procedures, improved specimen-transport and formal pathology-referral pathways, broader geographic participation, and progressive development of companion-animal cancer registration are needed to strengthen the national evidence base.

## ABSTRACT

Background: This study aimed to characterize mammary lesions in domestic cats through histopathological analysis, in order to diagnose the main types of mammary tumors and evaluate their distribution.
Methods: Sixty female cats, belonging to two breeds (Siamese and crossbred) and aged between 8 and 10 years, were examined between November 2022 and November 2024 in two provinces of Northeastern Algeria (Skikda and Sétif).
Result: Clinical examination revealed mammary lesions in 30 cats (50%). Histopathological analysis identified malignant tumors in 18/60 (30%), benign tumors in 9/60 (15%) and atypical hyperplasias in 3/60 (5%). Malignant tumors were the most frequent, with several histological subtypes identified, including complex carcinoma, tubulopapillary carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. These findings emphasize the predominance of malignant forms in cats, the diagnostic value of histopathology and the importance of early detection and preventive measures such as early ovariectomy.
